The withholding of revelation from the Prophet ﷺ occurred twice:

The first was before the revelation of the sūrah al-Muddaththir or al-Muzzammil, that is, after the revelation of two sūrahs or three of the Qur'an, according to the difference over which is earlier of the two sūrahs al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir. That pause is the one in which the Messenger of God ﷺ feared that revelation had been cut off from him, and after which he saw Gabriel on a chair between heaven and earth, as has preceded in the explanation of the sūrah al-Muddaththir. It has been said that the duration of the cessation of revelation in the first pause was forty days, and the polytheists did not notice it, because it was at the beginning of the descent of revelation, before news of it spread among them and before the Prophet ﷺ stood in prayer with the Qur'an at night.

The disagreement over the occasion of revelation of this sūrah indicates that it was not clear to the narrators. What we think is that the withholding of revelation in this instance lasted about twelve days, and that it was only for the sake of gentleness toward the Prophet ﷺ, so that his soul might be refreshed and his strength become accustomed to bearing the burdens of revelation, since the first pause was forty days and then the second was twelve days or so. Thus the revelation of the sūrah al-Ḍuḥā is the third descent, and at the third time, habituation to difficult matters is achieved; for this reason, the command is frequently given by repeating some acts three times. In this way, the various reports regarding the occasion of revelation of this sūrah and the occasion of revelation of the sūrah al-Muddaththir are reconciled.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 93, verse 4:

﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first (life).﴾

It is an conjunction ('atf) upon the sentence "Wa-l-Duha," so this is a statement begun anew, and the sentence is conjoined to the initial (ibtida'iyyah) sentences. It is not conjoined to the sentence that is the answer to the oath; rather it is an initial sentence. So when the abandonment (al-qila) was negated, he was given the glad tidings that his last state is better than his first, that his outcome is more excellent than his beginning, and that God is the One who concludes.

What is implied by the generality in the definiteness of "al-Akhirah" and "al-Ula" makes the meaning of this sentence, in meaning, a comprehensive concluding statement (tadhyil) that includes the continuation of the revelation and other good.

"Al-Akhirah" is the feminine of "al-Akhir," and "al-Ula" is the feminine of "al-Awwal." The term "al-Akhirah" in the terminology of the Qur'an has come to denote the Hereafter life and the Abode of the Hereafter, just as the term "al-Ula" has come to denote the life of people that precedes the ending of this world. So it is permissible that the intended meaning here, from both terms, is both of their meanings. It then conveys that the life of the Hereafter is better for him than this hastening life, giving him glad tidings of eternal good. It also conveys that his states proceed by moving from one state to another better than it. Thus the feminine form of the two descriptors runs according to both the case of predominance (taghlib) and the case of description (tawsif), and the feminine in this second sense is for the sake of observing the meaning of "state" (halah).

This alludes to the fact that the return of the descent of revelation to him this time is better than the return that preceded it; that is, God guaranteed that the descent of revelation would not be cut off from him thereafter.

The lam in "al-Akhirah" and "al-Ula" is the lam of the genus (lam al-jins), meaning: every deferred matter of his is better than its immediate counterpart, in this world and in the other.

The lam in His saying "laka" is the lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas), meaning: good specific to you, and it includes everything that relates to the Prophet's own self, in his person, in his religion, and in his community. This is thus a promise from God that He will spread the religion of Islam and enable his community to attain the good things which the Prophet ﷺ hopes for them. And it has been narrated

صفحة ٣٩٨
by al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'There was shown to me what will be opened to my community after me, and it gladdened me, so God the Exalted revealed (﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾)."

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 93, verse 5:

﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be content.﴾

This is likewise a conjunction ('atf) to the entire oath clause (jumlat al-qasam), and the particle of futurity (harf al-istiqbal) *sawfa* serves to convey that this promised bestowal is continuous and does not cease, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: (﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾ [Yusuf: 98]) in Surat Yusuf, and in His saying: (﴿and he will surely be pleased﴾ [al-Layl: 21]) in Surat al-Layl.

The second object of *yu'tika* (He gives you) is omitted so that it encompasses everything of good that the Prophet ﷺ hopes for, for himself and for his community. Thus the meaning of this sentence is the generalization of the giving, just as the sentence before it conveyed the generalization of the times.

The fa' of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib) is used in *fa-tarda* (and so you will be content) to convey that the bestowal is of immediate benefit, such that the recipient's contentment is attained upon the giving itself, and its benefit is not awaited after a period of waiting.

The definite form of *Rabbuka* (your Lord) is by way of idafa (annexation to a pronoun), rather than the proper name Allah, because of the tenderness and kindness that the word *Rabb* implies, and in order to reach its annexation to the pronoun of the addressee. In this there is an indication of His care for His Messenger and an honouring of him by annexing *Rabb* to his pronoun.

This is a promise of wide scope, encompassing what the Prophet ﷺ was given of victory and triumph over his enemies on the day of Badr and on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, the entry of people into the religion in multitudes, and what was opened to the Rightly-Guided Caliphs and those after them of the regions of the earth, east and west.

Know that the lam in (﴿and the Hereafter is better for you﴾ [al-Duha: 4]) and in (﴿and your Lord will surely give you﴾) — the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) was decisive that it is *lam al-ibtida'* (the lam of initiation), and he estimated an omitted subject (mubtada'). The estimate is: "And you, indeed, your Lord will surely give you." He said: the lam of the oath (lam al-qasam) does not enter upon the present-tense verb except with the *nun al-tawkid* (the emphatic nun), and since it is determined that the lam is the lam of initiation, and the lam of initiation enters only upon a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) of subject and predicate, the estimate of the subject is required. Ibn al-Hajib preferred that the lam in (﴿and your Lord will surely give you﴾) is *lam al-tawkid* (the lam of emphasis) — meaning the lam that is obligatory with the oath — and Ibn Hisham agreed with him in *Mughni al-Labib*. His words indicate that the presence of the particle of futurity (harf al-tanfis) prevents the attachment of the nun al-tawkid, and therefore the lam is obligatory in the sentence.

[Page 399]

I say: that the presence of the particle of futurity necessitates that the lam be the lam of the answer to an oath (lam jawab qasam) is a matter open to consideration.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 93, verses 6–8:

﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ ﴿And He found you lost and guided you?﴾ ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient?﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought in as evidence for the realisation of the promise. That is, it is a promise that proceeds in line with the pattern of what came before, namely God's care for you from the beginning of your upbringing and His gentleness toward you in hardships, in a consistent manner. It cannot be taken as mere coincidence (sudaf), because coincidences do not recur, and it is known that this consistency is willed by God, exalted is He.

The purpose of this is to instil certainty in the hearts of the polytheists that what God has promised him will certainly come to pass, by analogy with what He reminded him of regarding the continuity of His gentleness toward him in the past, which they do not dispute. The hope is that they will give up their obstinacy and hasten to faith. Otherwise, that (obstinacy) leaves a displeasure in their souls and phantoms of fear troubling their thoughts. Along with this purpose, there is a favour bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ and a strengthening of his soul's assurance through God's promise to him.

The interrogative is rhetorical (taqriri), and the verb (yajidka) is the present form of (wajada) in the sense of "to find" or "to come upon." It takes one object, and its object is the pronoun of address. (Yatiman) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), as are (dallan) and (a'ilan). The statement is a figurative depiction (tamthil) of the state of making benefits easy for one whose affairs were difficult, through the image of someone who finds a person in distress, looking to whoever might help or relieve him.

The orphan (yatim) is a child whose father has died. The father of the Prophet ﷺ died while he was still in the womb, or at the very beginning of his life after birth.

Al-iwa' is the verbal noun of (awa ila al-bayt), meaning he returned to the house. So al-iwa' means causing someone to return to a dwelling. Its first hamza is the hamza of transitivity, meaning He made him one who takes shelter. The term al-iwa' has been applied, metaphorically or by way of metaphor (isti'arah), to sponsorship and the meeting of need. The meaning is: He brought you up to complete maturity and uprightness, and you were under a perfect upbringing, even though orphans usually grow up with defects, because they do not find anyone who attends to their discipline and takes care of their moral conditions. ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾ ﴿and as for the one who asks, do not repel [him]﴾ ﴿and as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim [it]﴾.

The first fa' (الفاء الأولى) is the *fa' fasiha* (the "eloquent fa'," which signals an implied condition).

The particle *amma* (أمّا) conveys an implied condition, whose sense is: "Whatever may be the case." Its meaning therefore points to another implied condition, which is the reason the *fa' fasiha* was introduced. The implied structure of the sentence is: "Since you know this and have acknowledged it, then you must thank your Lord." He then explains what this thanks consists of by saying: (﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾), and so on.

Here thanks has been made appropriate to the blessing for which thanks is due. The implied condition is understood as "if you wish to give thanks," because the gratitude for a blessing is naturally drawn out of people by the impulse of decency (*muruwwa*) in common custom. The sentence is introduced by the detailing *amma* (أمّا التفصيلية) because it is a detailing of the general thanks for the blessing.

Since *amma* carries the sense of "whatever may be the case," its response (جواب) is joined with the fa'.

(اليتيم) [al-yatim, "the orphan"] is the object of the verb (﴿do not oppress﴾). It is placed first to express concern for its matter, and for this purpose it is not given in the nominative. Along with this, the requirement of using a response to *amma* is fulfilled by separating it from *amma* with something, out of dislike of placing the fa' of the response directly after the conditional particle. It appears that they only required the separation between *amma* and its response by placing some element of the response's relations first in order to express concern for what is placed first, because the position of *amma* is never free of concern for the speech, a concern that is rooted in some parts of the speech. Thus the use of *amma* in speech is an effect of concern, and this requires that the focus of concern be some of the complements of the sentence. That is what they take care to place first. The same applies to placing (السائل) [al-sa'il, "the one who asks"] first, and placing (﴿the blessing of your Lord﴾) before its verbs.

These three blessings to which this detailing is linked are matched with three actions that correspond to them.

It is possible that this detailing follows the method of *laff wa nashr* (لف ونشر, "folding and unfolding," a rhetorical device) in its ordered form, which is what al-Tibi (الطيبي) followed. It also accords with the interpretation of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, who explained (al-sa'il) as the one who asks about religion and guidance. Thus his saying (﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾) corresponds without doubt to his saying (﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha: 6]). That is: just as your Lord sheltered you and protected you from the afflictions of deprivation that usually accompany orphanhood, so you should be one who honours orphans and is gentle with them. This is gathered into the prohibition of oppressing him, because the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (*jahiliyya*) used to oppress orphans. Also, because when He forbids oppressing the orphan, despite the many causes for oppressing him, [He implies that] oppression may arise from anxiety over his needs; the slips of the tongue come quickly, as Allah the Exalted said: (﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ [al-Isra: 23]), and He said: (﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾ [al-Isra: 28]).

*Qahr* (القهر) means domination and humiliation, and this is the fitting sense here. These meanings may be expressed by action, such as pushing and belittling by deed, and they may be expressed by speech, as Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾ [al-Nisa: 5]), and they may be expressed by gesture, such as frowning. So the forbidden *qahr* is the kind of domination that is not applied to anyone other than an orphan in such a manner. As for *qahr* for the sake of correction, such as disciplinary striking, it is among the rights of upbringing. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqara: 220]).

His saying (﴿And as for the one who asks, do not repel [him]﴾) corresponds to his saying (﴿And He found you lost and guided [you]﴾ [al-Duha: 7]), because being lost calls for asking about the way, so the one who is lost is counted among the category of askers. And the one who asks about the way may be subjected to the foolishness of the one who is asked, as Ka'b said:

*And every friend I had hoped for said: "I will not distract you; indeed I am preoccupied away from you."*

So Allah made the thanks for His guidance to the path of good to be that one should widen one's heart for those who ask.

Thus "the one who asks" is not restricted to one who asks for gifts, but includes every asker. The greatest of the Messenger's (ﷺ) activities was guiding those who seek guidance. This interpretation is also reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed people are followers of you, and men will come to you from the farthest parts of the earth seeking understanding of religion. When they come to you, enjoin good treatment of them." Harun al-'Abdi said: "Whenever we came to Abu Sa'id, he would say: 'Welcome to the bequest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

The definiteness in (al-sa'il) is the definiteness of the genus, so it includes every asker, that is, about whatever the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about in a similar manner.

The unfolding follows the order of the folding.

If (al-sa'il) is interpreted as one who asks for what is good (al-ma'ruf), then it corresponds to his saying (﴿And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 8]), and it would be an instance of *nashr mushawwash* (نشر مشوش, "disordered unfolding"), that is, one that departs from the order of the folding. This is the approach followed by al-Kashshaf (الكشاف, the tafsir of al-Zamakhshari).

*Nahr* (النهر) is verbal reproach, such as saying: "Get away from me." From the prohibition of *qahr* and *nahr* is derived the prohibition of what is even more harmful, such as insulting, striking, seizing wealth, or leaving someone in need. Forbidding the asker from violating the etiquettes of asking in Islam is not included in *nahr*.

His saying (﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim [it]﴾) corresponds to his saying (﴿And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 8]).

Since enrichment is a blessing, Allah commanded him to make known the blessing of Allah upon him by speaking of it and proclaiming its thanks.

The intended meaning of (﴿the blessing of your Lord﴾) is not a particular blessing; rather, the genus is intended, which conveys generality in the rhetorical context. That is: speak of what Allah has bestowed upon you of blessings. Thus the blessing of enrichment is thanked within that command, and the command to thank for all blessings is also included, so that the sentence becomes a comprehensive conclusion (*tadhyil*).

If his saying (﴿And as for the one who asks, do not repel [him]﴾) is taken as corresponding to his saying (﴿And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 8]) by way of disordered unfolding, then his saying (﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim [it]﴾) also corresponds to his saying (﴿And He found you lost and guided [you]﴾ [al-Duha: 7]), again by way of disordered unfolding.

In that case the intended meaning of "the blessing of your Lord" is the blessing of guidance to the true religion.

*Tahdith* (التحديث) means informing. That is: inform [others] of what Allah has bestowed upon you, acknowledging His grace, and this is part of thanks. The discussion about placing the prepositional phrase (﴿the blessing of your Lord﴾) before what it governs is like the discussion about placing (﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾ and ﴿and as for the one who asks, do not repel [him]﴾).

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). The requirement of the command in the three places is that it be specific to him. The original sense of a command is obligation, so it is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) was obligated to do what he was commanded. As for addressing his community with this, it follows the principle of equality of the community with its Prophet in what is obligated upon him, unless some evidence indicates a specificity. Regarding the community's equality with him in forbidding the oppression of orphans and the repelling of askers, there are many proofs, together with what the principle of equality requires.

As for the community's equality in the command to speak of Allah's blessing, the blessings of Allah upon His Prophet (ﷺ) are diverse, and some of them are such that no one else in the community has any hope of them, such as the blessing of prophethood, the blessing of the Qur'an, and similar things that follow from the greatest chosenness. The blessing of "the Lord" in the verse is general.

So among the blessings Allah bestowed upon His Prophet (ﷺ), many must be spoken of, namely conveying to people that he is a messenger from Allah and that Allah revealed to him. This is included in conveying the message. He used to teach people Islam, saying to one who addressed him: "That you bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah."

Among them is his making people aware of the piety and obedience that are due to him, as in his saying to one who said to him: "Be just, O Messenger of Allah!" He said: "Would Allah entrust me with His revelation and you not trust me?!" Among them is also what falls within the speaking of blessing as part of the obligation of thanks for the blessing. For the Prophet (ﷺ), this obligation is free of any intervening obstacle, because the Prophet is protected from the intrusion of showing off, and people do not suspect him of that, so the obligation is firmly established for him.

As for the community, speaking of blessing may be accompanied by showing off or boasting, and it may break the heart of one who does not possess a similar blessing that is being spoken of. This is an area for examination regarding the conflict between what requires and what prevents, and the method of reconciling them if possible, or of giving preference to one of them. In the tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), it is reported that Commander of the Faithful 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the Companions, and he praised them. They said to him: "Then tell us about yourself." He said: "Gently, for Allah has forbidden self-praise." It was said to him: "Does not Allah the Exalted say: (﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim [it]﴾)?" He said: "Indeed I do speak. I used to give when asked, and when I was silent, I began [to speak], and within my ribs there is abundant knowledge, so ask me." Among the scholars, some restricted the blessing in His saying (﴿the blessing of your Lord﴾) to the blessing of the Qur'an and the blessing of prophethood; this was said by Mujahid. Among the scholars are those who held that speaking of blessing is obligatory. This was narrated by al-Tabari from Abu Nadra.

al-Qurtubi said: The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the ruling is general to him and to others. 'Iyad said in al-Shifa: "This is specific to him and general to his community."

From 'Amr ibn Maymun: when a man met one of his brothers whom he trusted, he would say to him: "Allah granted me, from the prayer last night, such and such." From 'Abd Allah ibn Ghalib: whenever he woke in the morning, he would say: "Allah granted me last night such and such. I recited such and such, I prayed such and such, I remembered Allah such and such." We said to him: "O Abu Firas, someone like you should not say this." He said: "Allah the Exalted says: (﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim [it]﴾), and you say: 'Do not speak of Allah's blessing.'" Ibn al-'Arabi also mentioned from Ayyub who said: "I entered upon Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, and he said: 'Allah granted me last night: I prayed such and such and glorified [Him] such and such.'" Ayyub said: "I tolerated that from Abu Raja'." It is also reported from some of the early generation (*salaf*) that speaking of blessing is for trusted brothers, among those one trusts. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Speaking of one's deed is done with sincerity of intention in the presence of those who are trusted, for it may otherwise lead to showing off and to thinking ill of one's companion. al-Fakhr and al-Qurtubi also mentioned from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali: "If you attain some good or do some good, speak of it to a trustworthy brother of yours." al-Fakhr said: However, this is only good when it does not contain showing off and when one does not think that others will follow one's example.

Surah al-Inshirah

It is called in most tafsirs, and in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, "Surat Alam Nashrah," and in some tafsirs it is called "Surat al-Sharh," and similarly in some eastern copies of the Qur'an, by naming it after the verbal noun of the verb it contains in His saying: (﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]). In some tafsirs it is called Surat al-Inshirah.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the twelfth in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Duha by consensus and before Surat al-'Asr.

From Tawus and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that they used to say: "Alam Nashrah is part of Surat al-Duha." They used to recite them in a single rak'ah without separating them, meaning in the obligatory prayer. This is an anomaly that contradicts what the community agreed upon regarding the division of the standard Qur'an into surahs.

The number of its verses is eight.

* * *

It contains a mention of Allah the Exalted's care for His Messenger (ﷺ), by Allah's kindness to him and the removal of distress and hardship from him, and the explanation of what was difficult for him, and the honouring of his station in order to relieve him. Its content is thus similar to being a proof for the content of Surat al-Duha, confirming him by reminding him of Allah's past care for him, illuminating the path of truth, and raising his rank, so that he may know that He who began with His blessing would not withhold His bounty from him. This was done by way of affirmation through a past matter known to the Prophet (ﷺ).

This is followed by His promise that whenever hardship comes upon him, he will find ease in his affair, in accordance with the way Allah the Exalted deals with him. So he should bear the burdens of the message and turn to Allah for His help.
